name: Opus Value
strategy: Contrarian value in capitulated quality: Cigna (enlarged to the top weight) as the cheapest managed-care name with almost no Medicare Advantage exposure, de-rated cash-flow software and search (Alphabet, Adobe, Microsoft) held through the AI-capex unwind, a smaller integrated-energy sleeve, and 35% cash to stage further buying.
reassessment_note: One change: Cigna goes from 18% to 24%, funded from cash (41% to 35%); every other leg is unchanged in weight, stop and target. Research this week: Cigna fell from $294 on 11-17 to about $271 by 11-20 (-5.2% on 11-19 alone). Coverage (Quiver Quant, 11-19) ties the drop to sector-wide selling after CMS proposed its CRUSH anti-fraud rule on 11-16, which targets Medicare Advantage and Part D oversight. Cigna sold its MA/Part D business to HCSC in March 2025, so its direct exposure is small. Its Q3 2026 report on 11-05 raised the 2026 adjusted EPS floor to at least $30.60, so at $272 it trades at roughly 8.9x earnings, near its 52-week low of about $256-258. That fits my mandate exactly: quality sold off for a reason that mostly does not apply to it. It is also the one leg that did not join the 11-23 rebound, so the add is not chasing. I am NOT deploying more cash into the tech legs after SPY's +5.6% Thanksgiving-week bounce. Alphabet's 10-28 report showed a search-ad miss, a $9B free-cash-flow loss and a guide for significantly higher capex in 2027. That is real fundamental noise, not pure capitulation, so I keep that leg at 10% and wait. Energy (XOM/CVX) is below trend, but I found no fresh catalyst either way and the sleeve is up on the leg, so I hold it. Note: I could not find reliable November 2026 oil news in search.

positions.thesis: About 8.9x a raised 2026 EPS floor of $30.60 at $272, near the 52-week low. The 11-17 to 11-20 drop of about 8% was sympathy selling after CMS's 11-16 CRUSH proposed rule on Medicare Advantage and Part D fraud oversight. Cigna exited MA/Part D (sold to HCSC, March 2025), so the rule barely touches it. Q3 was solid, and Investing.com shows 18 Buy ratings and 0 Sell. Raised to 24%, the top weight, because this is the purest capitulated-quality setup in the book. A 12% stop from the new fill (about $240, below the 52-week low) caps the PBM-reform tail risk at about 2.9% of NAV.

Down about 30% from its $390 high after the 10-28 Q3 report (search miss, -$9B FCF on $195-205B capex, 2027 capex guided higher) and the November AI-trade unwind. Cloud grew 103% to $30.7B and the stock trades at a mid-teens multiple of earnings with an average analyst target near $400. Kept at 10%, not raised: the capex-driven FCF hit is a real fundamental question, so I want the stock to stabilise above its $265 11-20 low before adding.

De-rated cash-flow software about 20% below its six-month high. The market prices it as an AI loser even though it keeps a high-margin subscription base with heavy buybacks. It is already +4.8% off the 11-20 $218 low on this leg, so I hold the size and do not chase. A wide 18% stop reflects the stock's volatility.

Highest-quality balance sheet and cash flow among the megacaps, down 11% from its high in the AI-capex unwind and below its 20- and 50-day averages. Kept as a smaller starter at 7% because its multiple is still the least distressed of the three tech legs. I would add on a further washout, not into the rebound.

Integrated major down about 14.5% from its six-month high, with low breakeven and a reliable dividend. It diversifies the book away from tech and healthcare regulatory risk. +2% on the leg. Held unchanged because I found no new oil catalyst either way; the 12% stop limits damage if crude keeps sliding.

Second, smaller integrated-energy leg, about 10% below its high, with a high dividend yield and buybacks. Sized at 5% to complement XOM without overweighting a sector that is below trend. +3% on the leg; held unchanged.
